newsitem.title: CANADA: British Columbia forest firms brace for labor talks.
newsitem.headline: British Columbia forest firms brace for labor talks.

text.p: British Columbia's ailing forestry companies will seek to keep a lid on their labor costs as they enter crucial negotiations next week for new contracts with workers in both the lumber and paper sectors.
The industry, which has sustained heavy losses over the past year due to weak commodity prices and high operating costs, hopes to head off strikes and job action.

But the stage appears set for a tough round of bargaining. The companies have said they cannot bear significant cost increases given their losses, while the unions are demanding wage increases and greater job security.
"It's going to be tense. The industry is struggling to keep its head above water...and can't stand any new costs," said industry analyst Charles Widman.

Industry consultants Price Waterhouse estimated that British Columbia's publicly held forest companies would lose C$450 million ($324 million) this year after a loss of C$250 million ($180 million) in 1996. The sector, which includes major exporters of wood and paper products, is the economic engine of the west coast Canadian province.

Closely watched negotiations with 29,000 unionized workers in the lumber sector start on Monday when the IWA-Canada union begins bargaining with Forest Industrial Relations, which represents about 65 companies on the British Columbia coast. The union's current contract expires at midnight on June 14.
"There is no doubt it will be a difficult set of negotiations as we expect the industry to try to hit us with everything they can," union president Dave Haggard said.
"Our membership is serious about reaching a collective agreement as soon as possible. It is not our intention to still be negotiating when Christmas comes around."
The IWA-Canada union will also meet later with the bargaining agents for companies in the interior of the province, but the coastal contract acts as a benchmark for all regions.
The union has already sparred with MacMillan Bloedel Ltd over its attempt to bargain separately with workers at each of its mills. The company dropped that plan last month after the union fought it.
The most contentious issue in the lumber talks will likely be a union demand to shorten the work week to 36 hours from 40 hours with no decrease in pay.
"It's going to be a big stumbling block. It would be a very, very large cost and one we are not prepared to assume," said Keith Bennett, the chief bargainer for the companies.
The union is also seeking protection from contracting out work and greater job security in the wake of closings and financial problems at several operations in the province.

British Columbia is a major exporter of lumber to the United States and Japan. The province sells about 9.5 billion board feet of lumber to the United States a year or about 20 percent of the market there.
The province's lumber industry has not experienced a full-blown strike since a 4-1/2-month walkout in 1986, but it was hit by wildcat strikes during negotiations in 1994.
In the pulp and paper sector, talks began in March between two unions and Fletcher Challenge Canada Ltd ( ). They are discussing a new deal to replace a contract that expired on April 30.

The Communications, Energy and Paperworkers union and the Pulp, Paper and Woodworkers of Canada union chose Fletcher as the target company for a pattern contract that they will then seek to duplicate at pulp and paper mills through western Canada. The unions represent about 14,000 workers in British Columbia.

Fletcher, the province's largest producer of pulp and paper, was also the target for pattern bargaining in the last contract talks and had a six-week strike in late 1994 and early 1995 before a deal was reached.
Neither side would comment in detail on the discussions under way, but analyst Widman said the unions were seeking a 12 percent pay rise over two years, a demand he called "totally unrealistic."
Job security and seniority rights during layoffs are also issues in the talks.

A Fletcher spokeswoman said that the two sides were continuing to meet and had exchanged agendas. Analysts said it would be many weeks before the talks hit their crunch phase and any strike would be months away.
((Reuters Vancouver Bureau (604) 664-7314))
